subject: mathematics

sections.title: The Dawn of Mathematics: The Human Need to Count
The Indian Context: Trade and Astronomy
The Revolution of Śhūnya: When Nothing Became Something
From Philosophy to Mathematics: The Concept of Śhūnyatā
The Bakhśhālī Manuscript and Brahmagupta’s Rules
The Arithmetic of Integers
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to explain why the product of two negative numbers is positive, by reading multiplication by a negative as the removal of a debt.

sections.title: Filling the Spaces: Fractions and Rational Numbers
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to explain why the denominator q must be non-zero in the definition of a rational number, how to equalise denominators before adding or subtracting two rational numbers, and to verify the distributive law for rational numbers.

sections.title: Representation of Rational Numbers on the Number Line
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to locate 8/5 and –7/4 on a number line by dividing the unit interval into equal parts.

sections.title: Irrational Numbers
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student whether √2 can be written as a ratio p/q, setting up the irrationality proof that follows.

sections.title: The Proof of Irrationality of √2
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to prove that √3 is irrational by the same contradiction argument, and to judge whether the approach also works for √5, √7 and √(10/3).

sections.title: Construction of Length √2
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student how a line segment of irrational length can be obtained at all, then to extend the ruler-and-compass construction to √3 and √5 and generalise it to √n for any positive integer n.

sections.title: The Story of Pi (π) and Mādhava’s Infinite Series
Real Numbers: Decimals and Cyclic Patterns
Rational Decimals: Terminating and Repeating
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to work out the decimal expansions of 10/3 and 11/12 and observe how the digits repeat, and to explain why a decimal expansion terminates precisely when the prime factors of the denominator are only 2, only 5, or both.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Never-Ending Journey
sections.think_reflect: Asks the student to consider what the square root of –1 could be, given that no real number squares to a negative, opening the idea of imaginary numbers.

prose_summary: Section 3.1 introduces the natural numbers by explaining the practical human need to keep count before any written symbols existed, developing the idea of one-to-one correspondence through a herder matching one pebble to each cow, and naming the resulting set N = {1, 2, 3, 4, …}. Section 3.1.1 explains the earliest physical evidence of humans recording natural numbers, describing the Lebombo Bone from between South Africa and Swaziland with its 29 deliberate uniform notches dating back about 35,000 years and read as a lunar or menstrual counter, and the Ishango bone from near the headwaters of the Nile dating to around 20,000 BCE, whose three columns of asymmetrical notches group the primes 11, 13, 17 and 19 and appear to demonstrate doubling. Section 3.1.2 explains how the need for larger numbers grew with civilisation, describing the standardised weights and measures of the Indus Valley cities of Lothal and Harappa that supported trade with Mesopotamia, the Vedic naming of all powers of 10 up to 10¹² (parārdha), the Lalitavistara’s names up to 10⁵³ (tallakṣhaṇa), and the explicit use of powers of 10 in the Ṛigveda, which set the stage for the Indian place-value system and for the invention of zero. Section 3.2 introduces zero as a genuine number rather than a mere placeholder, explaining that although the Babylonians and Mayans used symbols to mark an empty column, they did not treat nothing as something one could add, subtract and multiply, and that this transformation came in the work of Brahmagupta in 628 CE. Section 3.2.1 explains the philosophical origin of that transformation, describing Śhūnyatā (emptiness) in the Upanishads and Buddhist literature and in Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras as the state of stilling all vṛttis of the mind, and how a culture that revered emptiness possessed the conceptual framework to welcome nothingness into architecture, literature and linguistics and finally into mathematics through Āryabhaṭa and Brahmagupta. Section 3.2.2 defines and states the operational rules for zero, tracing the physical symbol to the bold dot (bindu) of the Bakhśhālī Manuscript, then giving Brahmagupta’s definition of zero in the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) as the result of subtracting a number from itself, a – a = 0, together with his laws a + 0 = a, a – 0 = a and a × 0 = 0. Section 3.3 introduces the negative numbers and defines the integers, following Brahmagupta’s question of what happens when a larger number is subtracted from a smaller one, grounding the answer in commerce through the two states of fortunes (dhana) and debts (ṛiṇa), and forming the set Z from the positive natural numbers, their negative counterparts and zero, laid out to the left and right of zero on the number line. Section 3.3.1 states and justifies Brahmagupta’s five rules for adding and multiplying integers — a fortune plus a fortune is a fortune, a debt plus a debt is a debt, a fortune or debt minus zero is unchanged, the product of a debt and a fortune is a debt, and the product of two debts is a fortune — each read back into the debt-and-wealth situation it models, and asks the student to reason out why a negative times a negative gives a positive. Section 3.4 defines the rational numbers, first introducing fractions as parts of a whole and negative fractions as the additive inverses of positive ones (noting that the minus sign may sit with the fraction, the numerator or the denominator), then defining a rational number as any number expressible as p/q with p and q integers and q ≠ 0, denoted Q. It explains that this set contains the natural numbers, whole numbers and integers, that the representation is not unique so that equivalent fractions may be reduced by common factors, and that the standard convention is to use the co-prime lowest-term form. It then states Brahmagupta’s laws for rational arithmetic — equality by ad = bc, addition and subtraction over a common denominator, multiplication and division by the invert-and-multiply rule with the required non-zero conditions, and the commutativity of addition and multiplication together with distributivity p(q + r) = pq + pr — and establishes closure of the rationals under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and under division provided one does not divide by zero. Section 3.4.1 explains and constructs the representation of rational numbers on the number line, recalling how integers are marked from an origin at equal spacing and then giving the general procedure for p/q: divide the unit interval into q equal parts and move p parts right for a positive number or left for a negative one, illustrated with 3/4 and with the improper fraction 9/4 = 2¼ located between 2 and 3. It then defines the absolute value |x| of a rational number as its distance from 0, works through |5/3|, |–5/3| and |0| to show that |x| is always non-negative, and gives the distance between two rational numbers a and b as |a – b|. Section 3.4.2 explains and justifies the density of the rational numbers, showing that a rational number lies between any two given rationals, that one such number is always available as their average (a + b)/2, and that repeating this gives infinitely many rationals between any two points — then raises the question of whether the rationals therefore fill the number line completely, which sets up the next section. Section 3.5 introduces the irrational numbers by way of the historical crisis they caused, describing how Baudhāyana, composing his Śhulbasūtra around 800 BCE as a manual for constructing geometric fire altars, met lengths that defied fractions, as did the Greeks a few centuries later. Taking a square of side 1 unit, it applies the Baudhāyana–Pythagoras Theorem to get d² = 2 for the diagonal, and defines irrational numbers as those numbers on the number line that cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers. Section 3.5.1 proves that √2 is irrational, attributing the first such proof to Hippasus of the Pythagorean school around 400 BCE and introducing proof by contradiction as a technique in its own right — assume the opposite and show the assumption leads to a logical disaster. The proof is set out in eight steps: assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms with p and q co-prime, square to get 2 = p²/q², multiply to get 2q² = p², deduce that p² and hence p is even so p = 2k, substitute to get q² = 2k², deduce that q is likewise even, and conclude that p and q share the factor 2, contradicting the assumption that the fraction was in simplest form. Section 3.5.2 constructs a line segment of irrational length and locates it on the number line, marking OA = 1 unit, erecting a perpendicular at A, marking B on it with AB = 1 unit so that OB = √2, and drawing an arc centred at O with radius OB to cut the number line at P, so that P represents √2; it then asks the student to extend the construction to √3 and √5 and to generalise it to √n for any positive integer n. Section 3.5.3 explains a second famous irrational number, π, the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter, recounting Āryabhaṭa’s highly accurate approximation 3927/1250 = 3.1416 in 499 CE together with his own description of it as an asanna or approximation, Lambert’s formal proof of the irrationality of π in 1761, and Mādhava of Sangamagrama’s realisation in the 14th century that an irrational number needs an infinite sum rather than a single fraction, giving his series π = 4(1 – 1/3 + 1/5 – 1/7 + …) and explaining informally what it means to add infinitely many terms. Section 3.6 defines the real numbers as the union of the dense web of rational numbers with the irrational numbers that fill the remaining gaps, forming the unbroken continuous line denoted R, and introduces the decimal expansion as the easiest way to tell a rational number from an irrational one. Section 3.6.1 explains and derives the decimal behaviour of rational numbers, establishing that dividing numerator by denominator either terminates (3/8 = 0.375) or repeats (5/11 = 0.45̅), and justifying why repetition is inevitable: the possible remainders when dividing by a fixed denominator are finite, so a remainder must eventually recur and the division loops. It then shows how to predict the type without dividing, by factorising the denominator of a fraction in lowest terms — 3/20 becomes 15/100 = 0.15 by multiplying to make the denominator a power of 10 — and states that the expansion terminates precisely when the prime factors of q are only 2, only 5, or both. It then develops the reverse conversion into the form p/q in three cases: terminating decimals (0.35 = 7/20), pure repeating decimals solved by letting x equal the decimal, multiplying by 10ⁿ for the n repeating digits and subtracting (0.6̅ = 2/3, 0.45̅ = 5/11), and general repeating decimals solved by first multiplying by 10ᵐ for the m non-repeating digits and then by 10ⁿ for the repeating cycle (0.16̅ = 1/6, 2.357̅ = 1061/450, 2.4537̅ = 6073/2475), closing with a summary table of the two procedures. Section 3.6.2 explains cyclic numbers as a pattern hidden inside rational decimals, taking the repeating block 142857 of 1/7 and showing that multiplying it by each of the digits 1 through 6 permutes the same six digits cyclically. Section 3.6.3 explains the contrasting decimal signature of irrational numbers — expansions that never end and never repeat, with no cyclic block, illustrated by √2 = 1.4142135623730950488… and π = 3.1415926535897932384… The section closes by noting the non-uniqueness of decimal representation, that every terminating decimal has an alternative form ending in repeating nines, so that 1.000… = 0.999… and 2.47000… = 2.46999… Section 3.7 summarises the chapter’s journey and represents the whole number system as a nested structure, recalling the notches of the Ishango bone, the philosophical Śhūnya of ancient India, Brahmagupta’s debts and negative numbers, the density of the fractions and the irrationals interspersed among them, and setting out the evolution N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q, the separate set of irrationals I, and their union as the real numbers R on which every physical measurement has a home. It then poses whether the journey ends, and introduces imaginary numbers denoted by i to handle √–1, which cannot exist on the real number line, noting their necessity in electrical engineering, quantum mechanics and modern technology while deferring their study to a later year.

enumerated_worked_examples.description: Evaluates the absolute values |5/3|, |–5/3| and |0| to show that the absolute value of a positive number is itself, that of a negative number is its positive value, and that |x| is always non-negative.
Divides 3 by 8 to obtain the terminating decimal 0.375, illustrating the case where long division eventually leaves remainder 0.
Divides 5 by 11 to obtain the non-terminating repeating decimal 0.454545… = 0.45̅, illustrating the case where the digits begin to loop.
Converts the terminating decimal 0.35 into the form p/q as 35/100 = 7/20.
Converts the pure repeating decimal 0.6̅ into p/q by setting x = 0.6̅, multiplying by 10, subtracting, and solving 9x = 6 to get 2/3.
Converts the pure repeating decimal 0.45̅ into p/q by multiplying by 100 (two repeating digits), subtracting, and solving 99x = 45 to get 5/11.

Converts the general repeating decimal 0.16̅ into p/q by first multiplying by 10 to clear the single non-repeating digit, multiplying by 10 again for one repeating cycle, subtracting to get 90x = 15, and solving to obtain 1/6.
Converts 2.357̅ into p/q by multiplying by 100 for the two non-repeating digits and by 10 for the one repeating digit, subtracting to get 900x = 2122, and solving to obtain 1061/450.
Converts 2.4537̅ into p/q by multiplying by 100 for the two non-repeating digits and by 100 again for the two repeating digits, subtracting to get 9900x = 24292, and solving to obtain 6073/2475.

enumerated_exercises.description: A merchant at Lothal receives 15 copper ingots for every 2 bags of spices; the student finds how many ingots 12 bags fetch, using proportional reasoning with natural numbers.
Identifies what the Ishango bone column 11, 13, 17, 19 has in common and lists the next three numbers fitting the pattern.
Given that the natural numbers are closed under addition, decides whether they are closed under subtraction and justifies the answer with a couple of examples.
A temperature in Ladakh of 4 °C at noon falls by 15 °C by midnight; the student finds the midnight temperature as a negative integer.
A spice trader takes a debt of ₹850, makes a profit of ₹1,200, then incurs a loss of ₹450; the student writes the sequence as an integer equation and computes the final financial standing.
Computes four signed-number results using Brahmagupta’s laws: (i) (–12) × 5, (ii) (–8) × (–7), (iii) 0 – (–14), (iv) (–20) ÷ 4.
Explains, through a real-world debt example, why subtracting a negative number is the same as adding a positive one, e.g. 10 – (–5) = 15.
Proves four pairs of rational numbers equal using the cross-multiplication test ad = bc: (i) 2/3 and 4/6, (ii) 5/4 and 10/8, (iii) –3/5 and –6/10, (iv) 6/9 and 2/3.
Finds three sums of rational numbers with unlike denominators, including one with a negative term: (i) 2/5 + 3/10, (ii) 7/12 + 5/8, (iii) –4/7 + 3/14.
Finds three differences of rational numbers, the third involving subtraction of a negative: (i) 5/6 – 1/4, (ii) 11/8 – 3/4, (iii) –7/9 – (–2/3).
Finds three products of rational numbers, including a negative factor: (i) 2/3 × 3/10, (ii) 7/11 × 5/8, (iii) –4/7 × 5/14.
Finds three quotients of rational numbers using the invert-and-multiply rule, including a negative dividend: (i) 2/3 ÷ 3/10, (ii) 7/11 ÷ 5/8, (iii) –4/7 ÷ 5/14.
Shows that (1/2 + 3/4) × 8/3 equals 1/2 × 8/3 + 3/4 × 8/3, verifying distributivity over a specific set of rational numbers.
Simplifies a bracketed difference of two rational numbers multiplied by a third, using the distributive property rather than direct computation.
Finds the rational number x satisfying a linear equation in which the distributive property must first be used to expand a bracketed rational expression.
Represents 2/3, –5/4 and 1½ on a single number line by dividing unit intervals into equal parts.
Finds three distinct rational numbers lying strictly between –1/2 and 1/4, exercising the density property.
Simplifies an expression combining the absolute values |–1/4| and |5/12|.
A tailor with 15¾ metres of silk needs 2¼ metres per kurta; the student divides mixed-number rationals to find exactly how many kurtas can be made.
Finds three rational numbers lying between the decimals 3.1415 and 3.1416, applying density to very close values.

Decides, without long division, which of 7/20, 4/15 and 13/250 have terminating decimals and which repeat, using the prime factors of the denominator, then verifies by carrying out the long divisions.
Performs the long division for 1/13, identifies the repeating block, and checks whether 2/13, 3/13, 4/13 and so on show the same cyclic digit behaviour.

Classifies six numbers as rational or irrational — √81, √12, 0.33333…, 0.123451234512345…, 1.01001000100001… and 23.560185612239874790120 — and writes the explicit fraction for those that are rational.
Uses the algebraic multiply-and-subtract method (let x = 0.9̅, multiply by 10, subtract) to explain why 0.9̅ is exactly equal to 1.
Converts 3/50 and 2/9 into decimals by long division, deciding in each case whether the result terminates or is non-terminating and repeating.
Proves that √5 is an irrational number, reproducing the proof-by-contradiction argument developed for √2.
Converts nine decimal numbers into the form p/q — 12.6̅, 0.0120̅, 3.052̅, 1.235̅, 0.23̅, 2.05̅, 2.125, 3.125 and 2.1625 — mixing terminating, pure repeating and general repeating cases.
Locates the decimals 0.532 and 1.15 on the number line, which requires reading each decimal as a rational number and then subdividing the unit interval.
Finds six rational numbers between the integers 3 and 4.
Finds five rational numbers between 2/5 and 3/5, where the denominators already agree.
Finds five rational numbers between 1/6 and 2/5, where the denominators must first be equalised.
Solves x/3 + x/5 = 16/15 for the rational number x by adding rational expressions with unlike denominators.
Given non-zero rational numbers a and b with a + 1/b = 0, determines whether the product ab is positive or negative without assigning numerical values, and justifies the answer from the sign rules.

Shows that a rational number whose terminating decimal has its last non-zero digit in the fourth decimal place can be written as p/10⁴ with p not divisible by 10, and reasons about whether the lowest-form denominator must be divisible by 2⁴ or 5⁴.
Determines, without dividing, whether the decimal expansion of 18/125 terminates and, if so, how many decimal places it has.
Explains how many decimal places the expansion of a rational number in lowest form with denominator 2³ × 5 will have.
Finds the lengths of the hypotenuses of all the right triangles in the square root spiral of Fig. 3.14, generating a succession of irrational lengths √2, √3, √4, …
